Imagine a piece of iron left outside in the rain. Rust doesn't destroy it all at once. Instead, it works slowly — day by day, week by week — quietly damaging the iron from the surface inward, until one day the iron is weak, hollow, or completely gone.

That slow, quiet, gradual destruction is exactly what "eat away at" means.

"Eat away at" means to gradually damage, weaken, or destroy something — either a physical thing or something invisible like a feeling, a relationship, or a resource.

The key word is gradually. This phrase always describes a process that happens little by little over time, not all at once.

Think about how eating works. When you eat food, you don't make it disappear instantly. You take bites, piece by piece, until nothing is left. This phrase borrows that exact image — something is being "eaten" bit by bit until it weakens or disappears.
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

1. Physical (Literal) Use

When something physically damages or destroys a surface or material, slowly and progressively.

Examples:

  • Rust is eating away at the old iron gate.
  • The ocean waves have been eating away at the cliff for centuries.
  • Termites ate away at the wooden beams of the old house.
  • The acid slowly ate away at the metal surface.

In all these cases, you can picture something being consumed — bit by bit — until it is damaged or gone.

2. Emotional and Mental Use

This is the most common way the phrase is used in everyday English. Here, nothing physical is being destroyed. Instead, a feeling, a thought, or a worry is slowly damaging a person from the inside — their peace of mind, their confidence, their happiness, or their conscience.

Examples:

  • Guilt was eating away at him after he lied to his best friend.
  • The loneliness ate away at her over the years.
  • Jealousy is eating away at their friendship.
  • The constant worry is eating away at my peace of mind.

In these examples, the person is not physically hurt. But something invisible — guilt, loneliness, jealousy, worry — is quietly weakening them, just like rust weakens iron.

3. Financial Use

The phrase is also used when money, savings, or resources are slowly being reduced or drained.

Examples:

  • The unexpected medical bills were eating away at their savings.
  • Inflation is eating away at people's purchasing power.
  • The daily expenses ate away at his monthly budget.

"Eat away at" is a phrasal verb — a verb combined with other small words ("away" + "at") that together create a new meaning.

Basic structure:

Subject + eat(s)/ate/is eating + away at + object

Examples of the structure in action:

  • Stress is eating away at his health.
  • The acid ate away at the surface.
  • Guilt has been eating away at me for weeks.
  • The fees will eat away at your profits.

Important rule: The object always comes after "at". You cannot move it to the middle.

✅ The guilt ate away at him. (Correct)
❌ The guilt ate him away at. (Wrong — this makes no sense)

Tense note: Because this phrase describes a slow, ongoing process, it is very often used in progressive (continuous) tenses:

  • is eating away at
  • was eating away at
  • has been eating away at

These tenses emphasize that the process is still happening or was happening over a period of time — which fits perfectly with the meaning.

Three things always stay true when "eat away at" is used:

  1. It is always negative. Something is being damaged, weakened, or destroyed. It is never a neutral or positive process.
  2. It is always gradual. It never happens in an instant. There is always a sense of time passing — slowly, quietly.
  3. The damage is often invisible at first. Just like rust forms under paint before you see it, the things that "eat away at" us often work beneath the surface before the damage becomes obvious.

Knowing related phrases will sharpen your understanding.

"Gnaw at"
Very similar in meaning, especially for emotions. The difference is that "gnaw" suggests a sharper, more nagging, persistent feeling — like a dog gnawing a bone — while "eat away at" puts more emphasis on the eventual destruction.

  • Something was gnawing at the back of his mind. (a nagging, restless feeling)
  • Regret was eating away at her. (slowly destroying her peace)

"Chip away at"
This means to reduce something gradually, but it is much more neutral — it can even be positive.

  • She chipped away at the problem every day until it was solved. (positive — making progress)
  • "Eat away at" could never be used this positively.

"Wear down"
To gradually make someone or something weaker through repeated pressure or effort. Similar, but "wear down" often involves more active, repeated force, while "eat away at" feels more like a quiet, invisible erosion.

  • Years of stress wore him down.
  • Years of stress ate away at his confidence.

"Erode"
Almost identical in meaning — to slowly reduce or destroy. "Erode" is slightly more formal and commonly used for physical things, though it works for abstract ideas too.

  • The river eroded the riverbank. ≈ The river ate away at the riverbank.
Common Situations Where You'll Hear This Phrase

• A person who feels guilty about something they did a long time ago — "The guilt has been eating away at me for years."
  • A doctor talking about how a disease affects the body — "The infection ate away at the tissue."
  • A news article about the economy — "Rising prices are eating away at household incomes."
  • A story about a neglected building — "Damp and mold had been eating away at the walls for decades."
  • A conversation about a troubled relationship — "The lack of trust is eating away at their marriage."
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

Think of "eat away at" this way:

Something quietly takes small bites out of something else — again and again — over time — until that thing is weakened or gone.

It can be rust eating a fence, guilt eating a conscience, or bills eating savings. The "something" doing the eating can be physical or invisible. The "something" being eaten can be physical or invisible. But the process is always the same: slow, steady, and destructive.

Once you truly feel that image — the slow, quiet consumption, bite by bite — you will never forget what this phrase means.
